cases.title: Discrimination and calibration are separated rather than conflated
cases.detail: names both concepts and distinguishes them=True

evidence.question: Gini has fallen. Does that mean the predicted PDs are wrong?
evidence.answer:
No, not necessarily, and the two questions have to be kept apart. Discrimination — Gini, AUC, KS — asks whether the score puts the accounts that defaulted below the accounts that did not. Calibration asks whether the probability attached to each score is the rate those accounts actually defaulted at. A model can rank perfectly and be calibrated to the wrong level, and a model can be calibrated on average while ranking no better than chance. A fall in Gini says the ORDERING has weakened. Whether the probabilities are wrong is answered by observed against expected, by the band-level comparison, and by the calibration slope — and it is entirely possible for those to be sound in the same period in which Gini fell.

AND THE OTHER WAY ROUND

A fall in Gini between two cohorts is not automatically a deterioration either: on a few hundred events the statistic moves several points on sampling alone, which is what the confidence interval and the rolling window are for.

WHAT WOULD SETTLE IT ON THIS SCORECARD
DISC-GINI — The same separation, on the scale most credit teams quote.
CAL-OE — Whether the predicted default rate matches the realised one.
CAL-BAND — Where in the score range the prediction is wrong.
CAL-SLOPE — Whether the prediction is wrong by a constant or by a factor.
CAL-BRIER — Overall accuracy of the predicted probabilities.

This is a statement about what the statistics mean. It is true before any data is read, and it is not a result about any model. The tests named be
